items.q: The osmolal gap is defined as:
items.exp: Osmolal gap = measured osmolality (osmomoter) − calculated osmolality. (Book p829)

items.q: Fill up: Calculated osmolality = 2(Na) + BUN/2.8 + ______ + 1.25 × EtOH (in mmol/L).
items.exp: Calculated osmolality: 2(Na) + BUN/2.8 + Glucose/18 + 1.25 × EtOH (in mmol/L). (Book p829)

items.q: Match the calculated-osmolality terms to their divisors — 1) BUN  2) Glucose  3) Ethanol … A) Multiplied by 1.25  B) Divided by 2.8  C) Divided by 18
items.exp: 2(Na) + BUN/2.8 + Glucose/18 + 1.25 × EtOH — BUN divided by 2.8, glucose by 18, ethanol multiplied by 1.25. (Book p829)

items.q: The normal value of the osmolal gap is:
items.exp: Normal osmolal gap < 10 mOsm/kg; a value ≥ 10 mOsm/kg indicates unmeasured osmotically active molecules. (Book p829)

items.q: A value at or above which osmolal gap indicates unmeasured osmotically active molecules is:
items.exp: Value ≥ 10 mOsm/kg → presence of unmeasured osmotically active molecules, e.g. methanol or ethylene glycol. (Book p829)

items.q: A patient with an unexplained high anion gap acidosis has an osmolal gap of 22 mOsm/kg. Which printed example fits?
opts: Diabetic ketoacidosis with a normal osmolal gap
Chronic kidney disease with urea retention
items.exp: A raised osmolal gap points to unmeasured osmotically active molecules, the printed examples being methanol and ethylene glycol — both HAGMA causes that also raise osmolality. (Book p829)

items.q: ‘The osmolal gap is calculated with the sodium term doubled and ethanol factored in.’
opts: True — 2(Na) with 1.25 × EtOH in the calculated osmolality
False — sodium is not part of the calculated osmolality
False — ethanol is subtracted, not added
True, but only when BUN is omitted
items.exp: Calculated osmolality = 2(Na) + BUN/2.8 + Glucose/18 + 1.25 × EtOH (mmol/L), and it is subtracted from the measured value to give the gap. (Book p829)

items.q: All but one of these belong to the osmolal gap section. Which is the odd one out?
opts: The calculated osmolality uses the chloride concentration
The gap compares measured (osmomoter) with calculated osmolality
A gap ≥ 10 mOsm/kg suggests unmeasured osmotically active molecules
Methanol and ethylene glycol are the printed examples
items.exp: The printed formula is 2(Na) + BUN/2.8 + Glucose/18 + 1.25 × EtOH — chloride is not part of it. (Book p829)
